segments.english: And as for what you wrote: "And more than this, what he wrote about the glory of the LORD that it is created light, if so, how were Israel going out at the entrance of their tents and bowing down to the created thing?" Not to the visible glory do they bow down, but only to Him who made His glory dwell there. And the visible glory is there as a sign and a token for them, for the Name, may He be blessed, desired the tent of meeting as His dwelling, just as we bow down and pray to the Name, may He be blessed, toward the Temple and Jerusalem, for the LORD chose Zion; He desired it as His dwelling. And the Rambam had already explained in chapter 64 of the first, that the glory of the LORD sometimes denotes the created light, which the Holy One makes dwell in the place, as "and the glory of the LORD dwelt on Mount Sinai, and covered it, etc." and sometimes by it they mean His essence, may He be blessed, and His reality, as in "show me, please, Your glory," and the answer came: "for no man shall see Me and live," which shows that the glory spoken of here is His very essence, may He be blessed, and he said "Your glory," to magnify, etc. And similarly we find in the words of our Rabbis of blessed memory that the name Elohim is equivocal, applying to judges and to angels, and to the Name, may He be blessed. Also, the name Shekhinah is equivocal, applying to what I mentioned above. And I saw fit to alert you here that there is no prohibition on bowing down to a man, so long as his intent is not to accept him as God, and he is not worshipped, but only submits to him and humbles himself before him, or by way of acknowledgment for a kindness that he did for him. For indeed Abraham our father bowed down to the sons of Heth for the kindness they did with him, to give him a burial place. And so Rabbi Saadia Gaon rendered: "and bowed down to the people of the land, to the sons of Heth, and prostrated to the people of the land that He created." And Joshua bowed down to the angel. And Nathan the prophet and Bathsheba bowed down to David. And we find much in the verses that they bowed down to the created being. And we read in Sanhedrin, chapter Four Deaths (Sanhedrin 61b): It was stated: "One who worships idolatry out of love and out of fear, Abaye says: he is liable, for he worshipped it. Rava says: he is exempt. If he accepted it upon himself as God, yes; if not, no. And Abaye said: How do I know this? for we learned: 'One who worships idolatry: one who worships, and one who sacrifices, and one who burns incense, and one who pours libations, and one who bows down, and one who accepts it upon himself as God, and one who says to him: You are my God.' What? Is it not that 'one who worships' means out of love or out of fear? And Rava says to you: No, but as Rabbi Yirmiyah resolves it: (Rashi explains: one who worships every worship that is customary for it, and one who sacrifices, etc., not in its customary way, and in every case the first clause and the last are for the sake of divinity). Abaye said: How do I know this? for it was taught: 'You shall not bow down to them; to them you do not bow down, but you bow down to a man like yourself.' One might think: even to worship like Haman? Scripture says: 'and you shall not worship them.' But Haman was worshipped out of fear! And Rava? Like Haman, and not like Haman. Like Haman, for he himself is idolatry; and not like Haman, for in the case of Haman it was out of fear, and here it is not out of fear. And Abaye said: How do I know this? for it was taught: 'An anointed priest in idolatry. Rabbi says: in an unwitting act, and the Sages say: in a concealed matter, and they agree that for a she-goat it is like an individual, and they agree that he does not bring a suspended guilt offering.' What is this unwitting act like? If he holds that it is a synagogue and bowed down to it, then his heart is with Heaven. But suppose he saw a statue and bowed down to it, (explanation: that he saw the figure of the king, which they were accustomed to make in the likeness of the king, and one who saw it bows down to it in honor of the king, and sometimes they worship it, and this one saw one who was worshipped and bowed down to it). If he accepted it upon himself as God, it is deliberate; and if he did not accept it upon himself as God, it is nothing. (Rashi explains: but he bowed down to him in honor of the king; it is nothing, for he did not intend idolatry). But is it not out of love and out of fear? And Rava says to you: In the case of one who says 'permitted.' Does 'says permitted' mean concealment of a matter? In the case of one who says permitted entirely; concealment of a matter is upholding part and nullifying part." Thus far the Gemara, with some of Rashi's explanation. And a matter is learned: that to every created being it is forbidden to bow down, except a man, provided that he not be worshipped like Haman, who made himself idolatry, (as we said in Megillah 19), for otherwise Mordecai would not have refrained from bowing down to him, as it is taught in the baraita: "You shall not bow down to them; to them you do not bow down, but you bow down to a man like yourself," provided that he not be worshipped like Haman, who made himself God, but one only bows down to him as a sign of honor, and not for divinity, and therefore Joshua bowed down to the angel, since he appeared to him in the form of a man, as it is written: "And behold, a man was standing opposite him," and therefore he bowed down to him as a sign of honor and not to worship him. And see in Sefer ha-Ikkarim, Treatise 2, chapter 28, where he elaborated on the verses that call the glory that appears to the prophets by the name YHVH, and also the ark, as it says: "And it was when the ark set out, etc. Arise, LORD, and when it rested he said: Return, LORD." And Joshua called the ark "Lord of all the earth"; see there. And in his view, that Joshua bowed down to the angel, because that bowing was in honor of the Name, may He be blessed, and since this one was His messenger, etc.; see there. And our Rabbis of blessed memory said: "Bow down to the fox in its time," that is to say: a man lowly and despised like a fox, and the moment stands for him in some office that is in his hand: bow down to him. And so it is customary with us and with the Arabs to bow down and kiss a man of high rank, and there is no prohibition in this, for he does not accept him as God; it is only as a sign of honor that he bows down to him and kisses his feet.

tokens.note: שכ' abbreviates שכתב, 'that he wrote'; the questioner's source is not named.
ה' is the Tetragrammaton as written: 'the LORD' (decisions, Names and titles).

tokens.gloss: the Name, may He be blessed
tokens.note: השי"ת: 'the Name, may He be blessed' (owner's default, Q3).

tokens.gloss: to the Name, may He be blessed

tokens.note: בציון is the verse's 'in Zion', rendered as the object of 'chose'.
בפ' is בפרק: 'in chapter'.
ס"ד is 64 in letter numerals.
מראשון: 'of the first'. The author names no book, so none is added.
הק' abbreviates הקדוש: 'the Holy One'; the author gives no 'blessed be He' here.
ית' (יתברך) follows 'His essence', where the Hebrew places it.
רז"ל is רבותינו זכרונם לברכה: 'our Rabbis of blessed memory'.
אלהים is discussed as a word shared by three referents, so it is kept as 'Elohim' and not rendered 'God' or 'gods'.
משותף (equivocal, said of a word with several referents) is the technical term of Maimonides, Guide I; here it is said of אלהים, which names judges, angels and God.

tokens.gloss: and to the Name, may He be blessed
tokens.note: ולשי"ת: 'and by the Name, may He be blessed', the third referent of the shared word.
Same term as 2:16.123: שכינה is likewise an equivocal name.
אהל: Judeo-Arabic ahl, "people of" (cf. עם הארץ in Gen 23:7); not Hebrew אהל, "tent". אלבלד is al-balad, "the land".
אלבלד is Arabic al-balad, 'the land', in a Judeo-Arabic rendering written in Hebrew letters.
שברא: 'that He created'. The subject of the verb is not marked in the Judeo-Arabic; see apparatus.
ס"א is 61 (the folio).
ע"ב is the side b of the folio: 'Sanhedrin 61b'.
ע"ז is עבודה זרה, 'strange worship'; here 'idolatry' (decisions).
פלחה is Aramaic for 'he worshipped it'.
באלוה: 'as God'. Under the doubtful-case rule the singular is 'God'; 'as a god' is the alternative.
לעבד is unpointed: "to worship" (לעבוד, the same root as ולא תעבדם in the answer) or "to a slave" (לְעֶבֶד). The English follows the first; the second is in readings.
כהן משיח is the anointed priest (Lev 4:3).
ביהכנ"ס is בית הכנסת: 'synagogue'.
אלא: "but". אנדרטא: "statue" (decisions give it).

tokens.gloss: in the case of one who says
in the case of one who says

tokens.note: יט is 19: Megillah 19, as the author gives it.
אלוה (singular, 'who made himself a god') is 'God' under the doubtful-case rule; 'a god' is the alternative.
שגאמר is the witness spelling for שנאמר, recorded here and not corrected.
ע"ש is עיין שם: 'see there'.

tokens.gloss: the Name, may He be blessed

tokens.note: ע"ש is עיין שם: 'see there'.

tokens.gloss: and our Rabbis of blessed memory

tokens.note: סגיד ליה: Aramaic, read as the imperative sense of the proverb, "bow down to him"; the fox is the one bowed to. A fox is despised, but its hour comes.
ר"ל is רוצה לומר: 'that is to say'.
והשעה: "and the moment" (Hebrew, in the author's gloss: "and the hour stands for him in some office"), not part of the Aramaic saying.

grammar: The paragraph is the respondent's reply in the correspondence of chapter 2. 'What you wrote' answers the questioner, and the question from 'And as for what you wrote' to 'created thing?' is his.

The main sense turns on the Bavli passage (Sanhedrin 61b), Bavli Aramaic, quoted from 'It was stated' to 'Thus far the Gemara'. Its Aramaic forms are glossed in the tokens (פלחה, קבליה, דהא, אי ... אין). The author's two Rashi glosses and his explanation of the statue are in parentheses inside it.
The Hebrew for 'not to the visible glory do they bow down' puts the negated object first. The English keeps that order, and 'but only' (רק) then answers it.
שהשרה is causative (made dwell): 'to him who made His glory dwell there'. The verse cited, Exod 24:16, is cut short by the author's 'וכו'', and the English keeps the 'etc.'.
Two verbs carry the argument: נעבד (passive, 'is worshipped') and נכנע ('submits'). The author separates bowing as worship from bowing as submission or thanks, so the English keeps the two apart.

Saadia's rendering of Gen 23:7 is Judeo-Arabic in Hebrew letters: וסגד לאהל אלבלד is Arabic 'and he prostrated to the people of the land' (אהל is ahl, 'people of'); the word שברא after it is unexplained.

משותף is the Maimonidean term for an equivocal word; the author says the names אלהים and שכינה each name several things, which is why a created thing may be called 'glory' and the bowing in Exod 33 is to the One who caused it to dwell.
segments.note: The reply quotes the questioner and the Gemara, and its Saadia and Joshua examples are kept as the author gives them.
apparatus: Base text: Wikisource. Its additions are translated as base text and flagged here until the 1931 scan is collated (decisions, Q2).
Exod 33:8 and 33:10 (the people rising and bowing down, each at the door of his tent), echoed by the questioner's 'יוצאים פתח אהליהם ומשתחוים'.
Ps 132:13 (embedded, no marks): 'כי בחר ה' בציון אוה למושב לו'.
Exod 24:16 ('וישכון כבוד ה' על הר סיני ויכסהו'), cited with 'וכו''.
Exod 33:18 ('הראיני נא את כבודך') and Exod 33:20 ('כי לא יראני האדם וחי').
Num 10:35-36 ('ויהי בנסע הארון ... קומה ה' ... ובנחה יאמר שובה ה''), cited with 'וכו''.
Josh 3:11 ('אדון כל הארץ'), the author's name for the ark, cited with 'ע"ש'.
Josh 5:13 ('והנה איש עומד לנגדו') and Josh 5:14 (Joshua's bowing).

Gen 23:7: 'וישתחו לעם הארץ לבני חת' (and the kindness of Gen 23:4, 'אחזת קבר'); Saadia's rendering (Judeo-Arabic in Hebrew letters) is translated from the words as they stand: אהל is Arabic ahl, 'people of'. The word 'שברא' is not clear; 'that He created' is the translator's reading and the alternative is not known.
1 Kgs 1:16 and 1:23 (Bathsheba and Nathan bowing to David).
Exod 20:5: 'לא תשתחוה להם ולא תעבדם' (the Baraita in the Gemara, and the author's quotation of it).
Witness spelling 'שגאמר' (2:16.559) for 'שנאמר', translated as the evident word; and 'לעבד' (2:16.313) may be read 'to worship' or 'to a slave' (see readings).
context: The anderta (אנדרטא) in the Gemara quotation is an image or statue; the author's Rashi gloss reads it as 'a figure of the king'.
The anointed priest (כהן משיח) of the Gemara quotation is the priest anointed for office (Lev 4:3).
Gen 23 tells of Abraham's purchase of a burial place from the sons of Heth (Gen 23:3-20).

readings.note: The unpointed לעבד may be 'to a slave'; the answer, 'and you shall not worship them', favours 'to worship' or 'to one worshipped'.
